headline: Great Point rip full of birds, but it's blues under them, not bonito — yet
subhead: Two weeks of watching the horizon for the first scout bonito, and Nantucket Sound keeps handing me chopper blues instead — for now.
body_markdown:
I had my hopes up Tuesday morning. Terns stacked three deep over the rip off Great Point, working a nervous push of bait right where the shoal drops from four feet to twenty on the last of the ebb, and for about ten seconds I let myself believe. Then the first fish came up and it was a chopper blue the size of a Duraflame log, not a torpedo-shaped bonito, and about forty of his buddies came with him. That's been the story of the last week and a half out here — the rips are loaded, the birds are working, and it's blues, blues, blues.

Not that I'm complaining, because the bluefish bite right now off Nantucket is about as good as it gets. Great Point rip on the last two hours of the ebb has been holding fish from five to twelve pounds, and they're eating anything that moves fast — Kastmasters, Deadly Dicks, half-ounce Hopkins in the chrome finish worked through the white water where the current stacks against the shoal. Sankaty's outer bar has been doing the same thing on the incoming, birds working the edge where the deeper green water meets the sandy shallows. If you want steady bend in the rod and don't mind losing a few lures to the teeth, this is the two-week window to be out there.

Striped bass are around, but they've gone quiet in the way stripers do when the surface water sits in the low-to-mid 70s the way it has been. I'm seeing very little daytime action on the Sound side — Horseshoe Shoal has been dead calm during the day, no birds, no boils, nothing worth a cast. The fish haven't left, they've just gone deep and nocturnal on us. My best intel this week has come from guys running the Monomoy rips after dark on the building tide, working big paddletails and bunker-colored plugs slow along the bottom edges where Monomoy Point drops into the channel. That's producing better-than-average fish, some pushing 30 inches, but you're fishing midnight to 3 a.m. to get it. During the day, don't waste your tide on the flats expecting a bass blitz — go find the blues instead and save the bass game for the dark.

Fluke have been the honest bread-and-butter fish all week, and honestly the most reliable thing I can point you to right now. The bite on Nantucket Shoals structure — the humps and edges south and west of the Great Point rip in 25 to 40 feet — has been steady rather than spectacular, which is about right for early August. Keepers mixed with plenty of shorts on white and chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets tipped on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the drift with the tide pushing you across the structure. Monomoy's flats on the harbor side have also been kicking out fluke on the last of the outgoing, working the channel edges where the sand drops off into deeper water. Nothing to write home about size-wise, but it's fish in the box on a day when the albie/bonito grounds are giving you nothing.

And that brings me to the fish everybody's actually asking about. Two weeks ago I said the bonito potential was building here right alongside what's happening in Buzzards Bay and around the Vineyard, tracking the same warm push. That's still exactly where we sit — building, not arrived. I haven't had a confirmed bonito crossed off the list yet off Nantucket, and neither has anybody I trust at the dock. But the ingredients are lining up. Water's been holding warm enough long enough, the tides are starting to load up as we work toward the new moon on the 12th, and that's historically the trigger that gets the first real wave of bonito and albies pushing up over the Shoals and into the rips at Great Point and off Monomoy. I'd bet on the week bracketing that new moon being when we start seeing real scout fish, not just birds and blues.

So here's what I'd do with my time this week. Mornings and evenings, work the Great Point and Sankaty rips on the moving water for blues — it's active, it's fun, and it's a guaranteed bend in the rod. Midday, if the sun's high and the rips go quiet, shift to the Shoals structure for fluke on bucktails and Gulp, slow and patient on the drift. If you're willing to burn a night, the Monomoy rips after dark on eels or big plugs are worth the lost sleep for a shot at a real striper. And keep one rod rigged light and ready — an Albie Snax or a small Deadly Dick on 20-pound fluoro — because when that first bonito shows up on the edge of the Great Point rip, and I think it's coming inside the next ten days, you won't get a second cast to make it count.
